Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology and risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Use patient history and physical examination findings to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome.
Discuss the role of supportive studies, including nerve conduction studies and
ultrasonography, in the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.
Identify the relevant anatomy and potential complications of carpal tunnel release.

Idiopathic median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel (IMNCT) is the most common peripheral
neuropathy in the upper extremity.
The symptoms and signs associated with IMNCT commonly are referred to as carpal tunnel
syndrome (CTS).
Advanced IMNCT results in loss of sensibility in the median nerve distribution of the hand,
thumb palmar abduction weakness, and atrophy of the thenar eminence.
Treatment options for CTS include bracing, corticosteroid injection (CSI), and carpal tunnel
release (CTR).

Overview
To demonstrate the divergence of IMNCT and CTS, surgeons should consider the
following: Surgeons have encountered patients with advanced IMNCT who did not have
symptoms until recently. Surgeons also have encountered patients with IMNCT who did
not have symptoms (incidental; ie, if a bilateral electrodiagnostic study identifies IMNCT
in the contralateral, asymptomatic hand).
Epidemiology
Estimates of the prevalence of CTS in the general population vary widely, perhaps partly
because of various definitions, measures, and diagnostic criteria.
As many as one-third of individuals may experience idiopathic compressive median
neuropathy at the carpal tunnel in their lifetime.
More women present with symptoms of CTS than men.
CTS often is bilateral.
Most median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel is idiopathic.

Epidemiology
CTS is the most common peripheral nerve compression syndrome diagnosis. The
reported prevalence varies notably based on the population studied and the criteria

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Median Nerve Anatomy
The terminal branch of the medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus; receives inputs
from C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1.
Travels with the brachial artery between the biceps and brachialis muscles and enters the
antecubital fossa medial to the biceps tendon
Branches of the median nerve
Anterior interosseous nerve: branches in the proximal forearm; provides motor innervation
to the flexor pollicis longus, the flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger, and the
pronator quadratus.
Palmar cutaneous branch: arises from the radiopalmar nerve approximately 5 cm proximal
to the wrist crease; provides sensation to the thenar eminence.
At the distal edge of the flexor retinaculum, the nerve divides into six branches: the recurrent
motor branch supplying the abductor pollicis brevis, three proper digital nerves, and two
common digital nerves supplying sensation to the thumb, index, long, and radial ring fingers.

Median Nerve Anatomy
Based on the anatomy of the median nerve, compression under the transverse carpal
ligament at the wrist leads to sensory changes in the thumb, index, long, and radial ring
fingers. In patients with more severe CTS, thumb palmar abduction is compromised
secondary to impaired abductor pollicis brevis innervation from the recurrent motor
branch dysfunction. Surgeons must recognize the variable anatomy of the recurrent
motor branch because this branch is at risk during CTR, especially if the motor branch
pierces the transverse carpal ligament (also known as transligamentous). The recurrent
motor branch is extra-ligamentous in 50% of patients, subligamentous in 30% of
patients, and transligamentous in 20% of patients.

Carpal Canal Anatomy
The carpal canal is defined by the scaphoid tubercle and the trapezium radially, the hook of
the hamate and the pisiform ulnarly, the flexor retinaculum palmarly (the roof), and the
concave arch of the carpal bones dorsally (the floor).
The carpal canal contains the median nerve and nine flexor tendons: the flexor pollicis longus,
flexor digitorum superficialis, and flexor digitorum profundus tendons.

Carpal Canal Anatomy
CTR involves division of the transverse carpal ligament. The transverse carpal ligament
has bony attachments to the ridge of the trapezium, the scaphoid tubercle, the pisiform,
and the hook of the hamate. The transverse carpal ligament is a mean length of 21 mm
from its proximal to distal edge. The bright yellow palmar fat pad marks the distal end of
the transverse carpal ligament2 (Resource 2).
Etiology
The exact etiology of CTS or median neuropathy is unknown and is likely multifactorial in most
patients.
Increased pressure on the median nerve affects nerve physiology and intraneural blood
supply.

Etiology
Normal carpal canal pressure ranges from 2.5 mm Hg at rest with the wrist in neutral to
30 mm Hg with the wrist in flexion. In patients with CTS, pressure ranges from 30 to 110
mm Hg. At 20 mm Hg, venous flow is disturbed and intraneural edema occurs, with
complete disruption of arteriolar and intra-fascicular flow occurring between 60 and 80
mm Hg. Prolonged higher pressure may lead to damage to the myelin sheath3 (Resource
3).

Risk Factors
Most median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel is idiopathic.
Some specific diseases add volume to the carpal tunnel, increase pressure, and cause median
neuropathy.
Rheumatoid arthritis
Trauma (distal radius fracture, perilunate dislocation)
Pregnancy
Amyloidosis
Other space-occupying lesions
The relationship between IMNCT and diabetes mellitus is less understood.

Risk Factors
Any condition that causes increased pressure in the carpal canal also may cause median
neuropathy CTS. Therefore, median neuropathy may occur in patients with rheumatoid
arthritis and flexor tenosynovitis and patients with a space-occupying lesion, resulting in
CTS symptoms. During pregnancy, 20% to 50% of women will report CTS symptoms,
typically worse during the third trimester. Although many patients improve after
delivery, as many as 30% of patients will continue to report CTS symptoms 3 years
postpartum3 (Resource 3).
The relationship between median neuropathy and diabetes mellitus is less clear. Both
are common, and a relationship is difficult to discern. Changes associated with
microvascular nerve perfusion are biologically plausible, and the glycemic changes that
may alter the subsynovial bursae and adherent tenosynovitis present in patients with
diabetes mellitus may contribute to nerve pathology. Patients with type 1 or type 2
diabetes mellitus are twice as likely as the general population to be diagnosed with CTS,
and as many as 80% of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus will be diagnosed with CTS
during their lifetime4,6 (Resources 4 and 5). Sensorimotor polyneuropathy often occurs
in patients with diabetes mellitus, and as many as 30% of patients with polyneuropathy
may have superimposed CTS6 (Resource 6).

The relationship between CTS and cardiac amyloidosis is an active area of research. CTS
often precedes the onset of heart failure or other manifestations of amyloidosis by
several years7(Resource 7). Cardiac testing performed 5 to 15 years after bilateral CTR
identified cardiac amyloidosis in 5% of patients.8 In select patient populations, 20% to
29% of patients undergoing CTR will have amyloid in the tenosynovium detectable via
Congo red staining,9,10 with a much smaller percentage having detectable cardiac
amyloidosis at the time of CTR. The natural history for patients with a positive carpal
tunnel tenosynovial biopsy with no detectable cardiac disease at the time of CTR is
unknown. Currently, no consensus exists with regard to screening criteria for
amyloidosis; however, male age older than 50 years, female age older than 60 years,
bilateral CTS, atrial fibrillation or cardiac arrhythmia, and spinal stenosis have been
associated with amyloidosis.11
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Intermittent or constant numbness and paresthesia in the thumb, index, long, and radial ring
fingers
Waking at night with hand numbness and paresthesia
With constant numbness (advanced median neuropathy), patients may have difficulty handling
small objects or buttoning buttons.
Patients often report worsened symptoms with holding a book or a newspaper, driving, and
other activities that involve wrist flexion.
Patients may describe a flick maneuver in which they attempt to wake up their hands by
shaking them out.

Patient History
Intermittent numbness in a median nerve distribution, waking at night with paresthesia,
and relief of paresthesia with shaking or repositioning the hands are the most commonly
reported CTS symptoms9 (Resource 9). Symptoms may be provoked by any activity that

places the wrist in flexion or extension, such as driving, holding a newspaper or book to
read, or blow-drying hair.
Physical Examination
Physical examination findings vary depending on severity of disease.
The following may be present in patients with advanced IMNCT:
Thenar atrophy because of wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis
Weakness of thumb palmar abduction
Diminished sensibility in the median nerve distribution
This may be assessed via Semmes-Weinstein monofilament or vibratory testing (threshold
testing). Threshold testing generally is more sensitive to changes in patients with early or
milder CTS.
Abnormal two-point discrimination occurs later in the disease course and may be indicative
of more severe or chronic compression.
Signs that may be present in patients with any degree of IMNCT:
Tinel sign: percussion over the median nerve, just proximal to the carpal tunnel, produces
paresthesia distally in a median nerve distribution.
Phalen maneuver: wrist flexion with the elbow in extension for up to 60 seconds produces
paresthesia.
Carpal compression test (also known as the Durkan test): compression over the median
nerve at the carpal tunnel for up to 30 seconds produces paresthesia.

Physical Examination
The diagnosis of CTS and IMNCT are difficult to study because no consensus exists with
regard to a reference standard. Even in the absence of a consensus reference standard,
consensus supports that no single physical examination finding in isolation is sensitive
and specific for CTS. Graham et al10 described a clinical prediction rule (combination of
patient history and physical examination findings; referred to as the CTS-6 evaluation
tool) for the diagnosis of CTS (Figure 1). Subsequent studies have shown a CTS-6 score
higher than 12 to be highly specific and sensitive for CTS, with electrodiagnostic testing
as the reference standard11 (Resources 10 and 11).

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies, such as radiographs, are not routinely indicated for the evaluation of CTS.
Side-to-side differences in wrist range of motion, fracture, or wrist deformity may be an
indication for radiographic evaluation.
MRI or CT is rarely indicated for CTS evaluation.
Occasionally, ultrasonography of the median nerve is used to evaluate the median nerve in
patients with CTS.

Increased cross-sectional area (CSA) of the median nerve (>10 mm2) at the level of the pisiform
is associated with CTS.

Imaging Studies
CTS has been associated with increased median nerve CSA at the proximal edge of the
transverse carpal ligament, which can be identified via ultrasonography or MRI12
(Resource 12); however, the exact role of either modality in the diagnosis of CTS is
unclear because studies have used variable parameters for location of measurement
and cross-sectional dimensions. A recent meta-analysis of carpal tunnel ultrasonography
for median neuropathy diagnosis identified a mean CSA of 11.6 mm2 for mild median
nerve compression, a mean CSA of 13.7 mm2 for moderate median nerve compression,
and a mean CSA of 16.8 mm2 for severe median nerve compression, with
electrodiagnostic studies used as the reference standard13 (Resource 13). Parameters
for MRI are not as well defined; however, a recent study by Ng et al14 found that a
median nerve CSA greater than15 mm2 proximal to the carpal tunnel correlated with
median neuropathy on electrodiagnostic studies (Resource 14). Although these imaging
study findings may support a diagnosis of median neuropathy, patients with these nerve
changes may or may not experience the clinical syndrome (meaning a collection of
symptoms and signs) of CTS. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-
Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
recommends against routine use of imaging studies in the evaluation of CTS.
Electrodiagnostic Studies
Some surgeons believe that nerve conduction velocity studies and electromyography cannot
detect meaningful pathology in early stages of disease because these tests evaluate only large
myelinated fibers rather than the small- to medium-sized fibers affected earlier in the disease
process.
Other surgeons believe that such unmeasurable disease would be very mild IMNCT, which is
managed nonsurgically.

According to the American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine, criteria
for median neuropathy at the level of the wrist include
Mild CTS: prolonged (relative or absolute) sensory or mixed nerve action potential (NAP)
distal latency with or without sensory NAP amplitude below the lower limit of normal
Moderate CTS: abnormal median sensory latencies as for mild CTS and (relative or absolute)
prolongation of median motor distal latency
Severe CTS: prolonged median motor and sensory distal latencies, with an absent sensory
NAP or mixed NAP or a low amplitude or absent thenar compound muscle action potentials.
Needle examination often reveals fibrillations, reduced recruitment, and motor unit potential
changes.

Electrodiagnostic Studies
No consensus reference standard exists for the diagnosis of IMNCT or CTS. Some
surgeons believe that patients may have notable and characteristic symptoms of CTS
with unmeasurable IMNCT. Other surgeons believe that this represents very mild
disease and is managed nonsurgically.
In patients with a high likelihood of CTS based on the CTS-6 evaluation tool,
electromyography/nerve conduction studies may have limited influence on the
probabilities of IMNCT and CTS15 (Resource 15). Electromyography/nerve conduction
studies may differentiate among cervical radiculopathy, polyneuropathy, cubital tunnel
syndrome, and CTS if a high probability of one or more of these alternative diagnoses
exists. Electrodiagnostic tests are not recommended in situations with notable
uncertainty (low probability) because a notable potential for harm is associated with
overinterpreting or misinterpreting the findings (Bayes theorem).
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Night splinting with the wrist in neutral helps limit paresthesia and waking (Resources 16 and
17). CSIs may afford short-term relief of symptoms (palliation); however, no evidence supports

that they are disease modifying.16

Nonsurgical Management
The role and value of CSI in the management of CTS is a subject of debate, with notable
regional variation based on surgeon preference. Comparison of the relatively limited
number of randomized trials on CSI is difficult because of the notable heterogeneity of
patients, the definition of CTS, control treatment options, outcomes assessed, and the
duration of evaluation.
In a recent prospective cohort study (no controls), 47 patients underwent CSIs for
electrodiagnostically confirmed mild or moderate IMNCT. Notable symptoms (Boston
Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire score ≥23) were present in 47% of patients 6 months after
injection and in 69% of patients12 months after injection. Nineteen patients (40%) of 47
underwent surgical treatment within 12 months of injection. Patients with diabetes
mellitus were more likely to have notable symptoms and undergo subsequent CTR
within 1 year of injection than patients without diabetes mellitus17,18 (Resources 18 and
19).
Oral NSAIDs and gabapentin have little effect on patient symptoms, and the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the
Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome does not support their use.
The oft-stated concept that response to CSI predicts response to surgical management is
not, to the knowledge of the author and editors of this lesson, supported by
experimental data. In a retrospective observational study of 54 patients who underwent
CTR (23 [43%] with a classic hand diagram and 34 [63%] with abnormal two-point
discrimination indicating advanced disease), only 15 patients (28%) had at least transient
symptom relief from at least one CSI;13 patients (87%) of those 15 experienced complete
symptom resolution with surgical treatment. Thirty-nine patients (72%) experienced no
relief via CSI, 29 of whom (54%) experienced complete symptom resolution with surgical
treatment.19 Diminished two-point discrimination (an indicator of advanced IMNCT) was
not associated with incomplete symptom relief. Patients who underwent surgical

treatment CSI had relatively advanced disease and limited response to CSI overall, and
only 34 patients (63%) of 54 experienced complete symptom relief with surgical
management. A study on objective measures of IMNCT (two-point discrimination,
electrodiagnostic tests) would aid in determining if the results compare with symptoms
of CTS.
Surgical Management
Division of the transverse carpal ligament arrests progression of IMNCT and relieves CTS
symptoms in most patients.
Patients with severe IMNCT who have numbness, weakness, and atrophy have permanent
nerve damage and likely will experience partial (rather than complete) symptom relief.
Paresthesia and/or pain often temporarily worsen after release of severe IMNCT.
Long-term results from open versus endoscopic CTR are comparable.
CTR may be performed with the patient wide awake with the use of local anesthetic and
without a tourniquet, with the use of local anesthetic and a tourniquet, or with the use of a
combination of sedation and a local anesthetic.
Postoperative immobilization is not necessary.
Prophylactic perioperative antibiotic agents are not indicated.

Surgical Management
CTR is the most common surgical hand procedure in the United States. Studies
comparing open versus endoscopic techniques have shown equivalent results for
symptom relief. The only documented differences between endoscopic and open CTR
are return to work and costs (Videos 1 and Video 2). Return to work is relatively
subjective for the patient and the surgeon and often is predetermined by the type of
work; the use of return to work as an outcome measure is questionable.20,21 The
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Appropriate Use Criteria on Carpal Tunnel
Syndrome may help guide CTS treatment options.

Complications
Transection of the recurrent motor branch
Median nerve injury
Scar tenderness, occasionally referred to as pillar pain, which generally resolves within 1 year.
Incomplete release with persistent or worsening symptoms

Complications
Variation in the location of the recurrent motor branch places this nerve at risk for injury
during CTR, especially in the 20% of patients who have a transligamentous recurrent
motor branch.
The incidence of CTS symptom recurrence after CTR is not well understood, and the
cause of recurrent or persistent CTS symptoms is a subject of debate.
Outcomes
More than 90% of patients report decreased CTS symptoms.
As many as 5% of patients report residual CTS symptoms 6 months after CTR.
Considerable improvement in sleep quality occurs within a few weeks of CTR.

Outcomes
Most patients experience considerable improvement in sleep quality within a few weeks
of CTR22 (Resource 20). Improvement of more advanced neuropathy may continue for
years and may remain incomplete23,24 (Resources 21).
